subject: Identifying NA value in an "if" statement

messages.author: c48a384dbad0597c
messages.subject: Identifying NA value in an "if" statement
parts:
Dear All,

In my earlier post ("Help for state space modeling using NIMBLE particle filter"), I shared my experiment for a state space model with two observations for each time step and got very helpful comments (Thank you!).

Now, I am trying to use the model to a data with missing values in observations (the same code is used, so I don't post here again). 

Using data with NAs, I realize that when I used the observation (i.e., y) of size N x 2 with a covariance matrix (i.e., R) of 2 x 2 with correlation, the parameters for R are not sampled correctly. Without the correlation, as expected, the diagonal term of R was correctly sampled. 

The R matrix was simply defined as:

R [1,1] <- pow (r11,2) # r11 & r22 are sd.

R [2,2] <- pow (r22,2)

R [1,2] <- rho*r11*r22

R [2,1] <- R [1,2]

rho ~ dunif (-1,1)


To figure this out, I filled the NA values with the means of the series (i.e.,  mean of y [,1] and mean of y[,2]), which is a simple method of imputation for missing data. Then I found that all the parameters were correctly estimated including the correlation parameters. From this, I conclude that the correlation parameters are affected by the missing data although NIMBLE seems to treat the missing observations well.

So, I added the following (in R script) to the "constants" to indicate whether each time step includes NA values or not:

is_Yfull = !is.na (y)

is_Yfull = is_Yfull[,1]&is_Yfull[,2] # TRUE or FALSE


constants <- list(

    t = nrow (y), is_Yfull=is_Yfull

)


Now, in NIMBLE, I used it as follows:


for (i in 2:t) {

   

    ...


   yf <- is_Yfull[i]

   if (yf) {

       # if both y[i,1] and y[i,2] have non-NA values

       y [i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[i, 1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])

   } else {

        # due to missing values in y, consider the on-diagonal only.

y [i,1] ~ dnorm(mean=x[i], sd = sqrt(R[1,1]))

y [i,2] ~ dnorm(mean=x[i], sd = sqrt(R[2,2]))  

   }


   ...

}


Some of you may find the problem with my code immediately, but the error message I get is:


defining model...

Error in eval(code[[2]], constantsEnv) : object 'yf' not found


I wonder if there is a correct way to treat the missing observations, in particular to estimate the correlation parameters of R. I would appreciate it if you could offer any thoughts or comments.


Thank you very much.


- Seongeun

messages.author: dd632bd3bbcdd7e9
messages.subject: Re: Identifying NA value in an "if" statement
parts:
Right now I'm just responding on the mechanics of the last part of your message.  Looking at what should be happening regarding missing data is another issue.

You can't use an if-then like that in model code.  You can use an if-then if the condition can be evaluated *once* when the model is created and any variables in the condition are R variables.  You can't have model variables in the if statement.  The reason is that nimble creates a static graphical model.

There are a couple of ways to get the behavior you want.  One is to write a custom distribution, but that probably isn't necessary here.  Another is to use something like

for(i in 1:N_full) {
   y[ full_indices[i], 1:2] ~ ...
}

for(i in 1:N_not_full) {
  y[ not_full_indices[i], 1] ~ ...
  y[ not_full_indices[i], 2] ~ ...
}

messages.subject: Re: Identifying NA value in an "if" statement
parts:
Hi Perry,

I appreciate your spending time on this.

Based on your advice, I changed the code separating the state eq. from the obs. eq. using different loops. It takes a longer time to compile but it seems to work!

# only the state variable
for (i in 2:t) {

predX [i] <- x[i - 1] + d
  x[i] ~ dnorm(mean= predX[i], sd = sigw)
  predY [i] <- x[i]
}

# observation only
for (i in 2:N_full_indices) {
  
  #----------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # Observation equation
  #----------------------------------------------------------------------------
  # observation model: yt = Axt + vt,  
  # where yt = [yt1, yt2]^T, A = [1,1]^T and vt = [vt1, vt2]^T
  X [full_indices[i], 1] <- x[full_indices[i]]
  X [full_indices[i], 2] <- x[full_indices[i]]
  
  y [full_indices[i],1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[full_indices[i], 1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])
}

for (i in 2:N_not_full_indices) {
  
  y [Not_full_indices[i],1] ~ dnorm(mean=x[Not_full_indices[i]], sd = sqrt(R[1,1]))
  y [Not_full_indices[i],2] ~ dnorm(mean=x[Not_full_indices[i]], sd = sqrt(R[2,2]))  
}


Thanks very much for your help!

- Seongeun

messages.author: 5fa2a363d4ddd1d1
messages.subject: Re: Identifying NA value in an "if" statement
parts:
Hi Seongeun,

Just a note to mention that you should in NIMBLE be able to use
y[ not_full_indices[i], 1:2 ] ~ dmnorm(X[not_full_indices[i], 1:2],

and NIMBLE would sample those y's from their predictive bivariate
normal distributions, if both elements of the two-element vector are
NA.
I don't know if that's what you want, but the MCMC should be valid. If
you think it is not, please provide us with a reproducible example.

We don't have a way, however, to handle a multivariate node that has
some NAs and some non-NAs, because NIMBLE can't sample
from the conditional of multivariate distribution for a subset of the elements.

Chris

Chris

messages.subject: Re: Identifying NA value in an "if" statement
parts:
Hi Chris,

Thanks very much for your additional comment.

Originally, I used both y[ not_full_indices[i], 1:2 ] and y[ full_indices[i], 1:2 ] using one "for" loop without using the indices constant, which I now added based on Perry's comments. When I used one loop only, NIBMLE compiled and ran, but the posterior parameters for the covariance (i.e., r11, r22) were not correctly updated (i.e., remain as the initial values). Yes, I could see that missing Y's were sampled in the predictive normal distribution; I understood this as imputation. But the problem was with the covariance parameters.

Please find attached my code and data to see if my observation is true or if the problem with r11 and r22 is due to other factors that were wrong with my code.

Thanks again.

- Seongeun

>>> y [i,1] ~ dnorm(mean=x[i], sd = sqrt(R[1,1]))
>>>
>>> y [i,2] ~ dnorm(mean=x[i], sd = sqrt(R[2,2]))
>>>
>>>    }
>>>
>>>
>>>    ...
>>>
>>> }
>>>
>>>
>>> Some of you may find the problem with my code immediately, but the error message I get is:
>>>
>>>
>>> defining model...
>>>
>>> Error in eval(code[[2]], constantsEnv) : object 'yf' not found
>>>
>>>
>>> I wonder if there is a correct way to treat the missing observations, in particular to estimate the correlation parameters of R. I would appreciate it if you could offer any thoughts or comments.
>>>
>>>
>>> Thank you very much.
>>>
>>>
>>> - Seongeun

messages.subject: Re: Identifying NA value in an "if" statement
parts:
Hi Seongeun,

The code you attached most recently looks fine to me. So if you think
it is giving you the correct answer, there is probably not a need to
delve deeper. As you and Perry discussed, we wouldn't expect the
original version of the code to work.

Chris

On Tue, Oct 9, 2018 at 7:26 PM Seongeun Jeong <jeo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>
> Hi Chris,
>
> Thanks very much for your additional comment.
>
> Originally, I used both y[ not_full_indices[i], 1:2 ] and y[ full_indices[i], 1:2 ] using one "for" loop without using the indices constant, which I now added based on Perry's comments. When I used one loop only, NIBMLE compiled and ran, but the posterior parameters for the covariance (i.e., r11, r22) were not correctly updated (i.e., remain as the initial values). Yes, I could see that missing Y's were sampled in the predictive normal distribution; I understood this as imputation. But the problem was with the covariance parameters.
>
> Please find attached my code and data to see if my observation is true or if the problem with r11 and r22 is due to other factors that were wrong with my code.
>
> Thanks again.
>
> - Seongeun
>
>
>
> On Tuesday, October 9, 2018 at 6:06:56 PM UTC-7, Christopher Paciorek wrote:
>>
>> Hi Seongeun,
>>
>> Just a note to mention that you should in NIMBLE be able to use
>> y[ not_full_indices[i], 1:2 ] ~ dmnorm(X[not_full_indices[i], 1:2],
>> cov = R[1:2,1:2])
>>
>> and NIMBLE would sample those y's from their predictive bivariate
>> normal distributions, if both elements of the two-element vector are
>> NA.
>> I don't know if that's what you want, but the MCMC should be valid. If
>> you think it is not, please provide us with a reproducible example.
>>
>> We don't have a way, however, to handle a multivariate node that has
>> some NAs and some non-NAs, because NIMBLE can't sample
>> from the conditional of multivariate distribution for a subset of the elements.
>>
>> Chris
>>
>> Chris
>> On Tue, Oct 9, 2018 at 4:51 PM Seongeun Jeong <jeo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >
>> > Hi Perry,
>> >
>> > I appreciate your spending time on this.
>> >
>> > Based on your advice, I changed the code separating the state eq. from the obs. eq. using different loops. It takes a longer time to compile but it seems to work!
>> >
>> > # only the state variable
>> > for (i in 2:t) {
>> > predX [i] <- x[i - 1] + d
>> > x[i] ~ dnorm(mean= predX[i], sd = sigw)
>> > predY [i] <- x[i]
>> > }
>> >
>> > # observation only
>> > for (i in 2:N_full_indices) {
>> >
>> > #----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>> > # Observation equation
>> > #----------------------------------------------------------------------------
>> > # observation model: yt = Axt + vt,
>> > # where yt = [yt1, yt2]^T, A = [1,1]^T and vt = [vt1, vt2]^T
>> > X [full_indices[i], 1] <- x[full_indices[i]]
>> > X [full_indices[i], 2] <- x[full_indices[i]]
>> >
>> > y [full_indices[i],1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[full_indices[i], 1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])
>> > }
>> >
>> > for (i in 2:N_not_full_indices) {
>> >
>> > y [Not_full_indices[i],1] ~ dnorm(mean=x[Not_full_indices[i]], sd = sqrt(R[1,1]))
>> > y [Not_full_indices[i],2] ~ dnorm(mean=x[Not_full_indices[i]], sd = sqrt(R[2,2]))
>> > }
>> >
>> >
>> > Thanks very much for your help!
>> >
>> > - Seongeun
>> >
>> > On Tuesday, October 9, 2018 at 9:59:30 AM UTC-7, pdevalpine wrote:
>> >>
>> >> Right now I'm just responding on the mechanics of the last part of your message. Looking at what should be happening regarding missing data is another issue.
>> >>
>> >> You can't use an if-then like that in model code. You can use an if-then if the condition can be evaluated *once* when the model is created and any variables in the condition are R variables. You can't have model variables in the if statement. The reason is that nimble creates a static graphical model.
>> >>
>> >> There are a couple of ways to get the behavior you want. One is to write a custom distribution, but that probably isn't necessary here. Another is to use something like
>> >>
>> >> for(i in 1:N_full) {
>> >> y[ full_indices[i], 1:2] ~ ...
>> >> }
>> >>
>> >> for(i in 1:N_not_full) {
>> >> y[ not_full_indices[i], 1] ~ ...
>> >> y[ not_full_indices[i], 2] ~ ...
>> >> }
>> >>
>> >> On Mon, Oct 8, 2018 at 12:01 PM Seongeun Jeong <jeo...@gmail.com> wrote:
>> >>>
>> >>> Dear All,
>> >>>
>> >>> In my earlier post ("Help for state space modeling using NIMBLE particle filter"), I shared my experiment for a state space model with two observations for each time step and got very helpful comments (Thank you!).
>> >>>
>> >>> Now, I am trying to use the model to a data with missing values in observations (the same code is used, so I don't post here again).
>> >>>
>> >>> Using data with NAs, I realize that when I used the observation (i.e., y) of size N x 2 with a covariance matrix (i.e., R) of 2 x 2 with correlation, the parameters for R are not sampled correctly. Without the correlation, as expected, the diagonal term of R was correctly sampled.
>> >>>
>> >>> The R matrix was simply defined as:
>> >>>
>> >>> R [1,1] <- pow (r11,2) # r11 & r22 are sd.
>> >>>
>> >>> R [2,2] <- pow (r22,2)
>> >>>
>> >>> R [1,2] <- rho*r11*r22
>> >>>
>> >>> R [2,1] <- R [1,2]
>> >>>
>> >>> rho ~ dunif (-1,1)
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> To figure this out, I filled the NA values with the means of the series (i.e., mean of y [,1] and mean of y[,2]), which is a simple method of imputation for missing data. Then I found that all the parameters were correctly estimated including the correlation parameters. From this, I conclude that the correlation parameters are affected by the missing data although NIMBLE seems to treat the missing observations well.
>> >>>
>> >>> So, I added the following (in R script) to the "constants" to indicate whether each time step includes NA values or not:
>> >>>
>> >>> is_Yfull = !is.na (y)
>> >>>
>> >>> is_Yfull = is_Yfull[,1]&is_Yfull[,2] # TRUE or FALSE
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> constants <- list(
>> >>>
>> >>> t = nrow (y), is_Yfull=is_Yfull
>> >>>
>> >>> )
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> Now, in NIMBLE, I used it as follows:
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> for (i in 2:t) {
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> ...
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> yf <- is_Yfull[i]
>> >>>
>> >>> if (yf) {
>> >>>
>> >>> # if both y[i,1] and y[i,2] have non-NA values
>> >>>
>> >>> y [i,1:2] ~ dmnorm(mean=X[i, 1:2], cov = R[1:2,1:2])
>> >>>
>> >>> } else {
>> >>>
>> >>> # due to missing values in y, consider the on-diagonal only.
>> >>>
>> >>> y [i,1] ~ dnorm(mean=x[i], sd = sqrt(R[1,1]))
>> >>>
>> >>> y [i,2] ~ dnorm(mean=x[i], sd = sqrt(R[2,2]))
>> >>>
>> >>> }
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> ...
>> >>>
>> >>> }
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> Some of you may find the problem with my code immediately, but the error message I get is:
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> defining model...
>> >>>
>> >>> Error in eval(code[[2]], constantsEnv) : object 'yf' not found
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> I wonder if there is a correct way to treat the missing observations, in particular to estimate the correlation parameters of R. I would appreciate it if you could offer any thoughts or comments.
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> Thank you very much.
>> >>>
>> >>>
>> >>> - Seongeun
